About this simulation

On screen
Left: the solar-neutrino spectrum at the Earth on log–log axes, energy 0.1 to 20 MeV and flux per MeV 107 to 1016 m-2 s-1 MeV-1. The pp, ¹³N and ¹⁵O (dashed) and ⁸B continua are curves; the ⁷Be lines (0.862 and 0.384 MeV) and the pep line (1.442 MeV) are vertical lines drawn to their total flux in m-2 s-1 on the same axis. A faint grey outline keeps the standard spectrum in place. Dashed lines mark the thresholds of gallium, chlorine and water; the part of the spectrum the selected detector counts is shaded. Right: each detector's model rate as a fraction of its standard-model rate against the central temperature, traced over the temperatures you have visited, with a dot at the current temperature and the measured fraction as a short tick at the right edge.
Controls
Detector selects gallium, chlorine or water; it never moves the temperature. The temperature slider sets the central temperature as a fraction of its standard-model value, 0.850 to 1.000, with the luminosity held at its observed value. Clear inset traces erases the traced curves.
Measured
Each source keeps its shape and its flux is multiplied by (Tc/Tc,0)n, with n = −2.4 (pep), 10 (⁷Be), 24 (⁸B), 24.4 (¹³N), 27.1 (¹⁵O), from BS05 standard-solar-model fluxes. The pp flux is then set so that the luminosity stays at its observed value, so it rises by up to 7 per cent. Detector rates R/R0 use Bahcall's averaged cross sections (not the drawn curves); measured fractions are Homestake, SAGE+GALLEX+GNO and Super-Kamiokande over their standard-model rates. The water value, 0.41, is Super-Kamiokande's; the earlier Kamiokande detector described in the notes found about half. The sidebar Readouts give Tc/Tc,0 and, for the selected detector, the model and measured rates. About 6.5 × 1014 neutrinos cross each square metre per second.
Conditions
The power laws hold only near the standard model, with the luminosity held fixed and nothing else about the Sun changed. The experiment is historical: the deficits were in fact explained by neutrino flavour change (oscillation). Electron neutrinos made in the core turn partly into other flavours, which these detectors count weakly or not at all, and in 2001 the SNO detector measured the full boron-8 flux of the standard solar model.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A slightly cooler core

Select the water detector and leave the central temperature at 1.00 of its standard value, so that the predicted rate is 1.00 and the measured rate is 0.41. Before you move the slider, predict the predicted rate of the water detector when the core is made five per cent cooler, at 0.95. Then set the temperature to 0.95.

2 · The gallium detector

Keep the temperature at 0.95 and select the gallium detector. Before you look at the readout, predict the predicted rate of the gallium detector at this temperature.

3 · Sweeping the temperature down

Keep the gallium detector selected. Its measured rate is 0.52 of the standard-model rate. Before you move the slider, predict what happens to the predicted rate as you sweep the temperature slowly all the way down to 0.85. Then sweep it down and watch the inset.

4 · Checking with chlorine

Select the water detector and set the temperature to 0.965, where its predicted rate of 0.43 is close to its measured 0.41. Before you change detector, predict how the predicted rate of the chlorine detector at this temperature compares with its measured 0.32. Then select the chlorine detector.

5 · Back to water

Keep the chlorine detector selected and lower the temperature to 0.945, where its predicted rate of about 0.33 is close to its measured 0.32. Before you select the water detector, predict its predicted rate at this temperature, compared with its measured 0.41. Then select the water detector.

6 · No single cooling fits

Water needs a core at about 0.964 of the standard temperature, chlorine about 0.943, and gallium cannot reach its measured rate at any temperature. Each detector counts a different part of the spectrum, and the three shortfalls do not share one shape, so a cooler core cannot explain them all.

The explanation lies in the neutrinos, not in the Sun. Electron neutrinos change flavour on their way out, and these detectors count mainly the electron kind. In 2001 the SNO detector, which also counted the other flavours, found the full boron-8 flux of the standard solar model.

Counting the Sun's Neutrinos

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Neutrinos made in the Sun's core leave it almost unabsorbed, and three kinds of detector count them. Each counts a different part of their spectrum. This sim cools the core and sets each detector's predicted rate beside the rate it measured.

What you'll learn

  • Which neutrinos each detector is able to count.
  • How each kind of neutrino responds to the core temperature.
  • How the predicted rates compare with the measured ones.
  • Whether one change to the core can account for all three detectors.
The set-up: neutrinos from the core reach three detectors, and each counts only the neutrinos above its own threshold.

What's on screen

  • Left panel: the neutrino spectrum at the Earth on log scales. The pp and boron-8 curves are solid, the CNO curves dashed. The beryllium-7 and pep lines are drawn to their total flux.
  • Dashed vertical lines mark the gallium, chlorine and water thresholds. The part of the spectrum the selected detector counts is shaded, and a faint grey outline keeps the standard spectrum in place.
  • Right panel: each detector's predicted rate against the core temperature, traced over the temperatures you visit, with the measured rate as a short tick at the right edge.
  • Readouts: the temperature, the selected detector, its predicted rate and its measured rate.
See itLook at the sim at its opening values. Watch for: the spectrum with dashed threshold lines, a shaded counted region, and predicted and measured in the Readouts.

03

Each detector counts above its threshold: three slices of one spectrum

The first reaction of the chains, p + p, makes most of the neutrinos, with energies below about 0.42 MeV. Boron-8 makes a few, up to about 15 MeV. A detector responds only above a threshold energy, so each samples a different part of the spectrum.

Gallium has a threshold of 0.23 MeV, low enough to admit the first reaction's neutrinos. Chlorine, in the tank Davis built, needs more than 0.81 MeV, so it counts the beryllium-7 line at 0.86 MeV and the boron-8 neutrinos. Water responds only to boron-8, above about 5 MeV.

The standard spectrum, sampled from the sim. The dashed lines are the thresholds, as in the notes' Figure 59.

Each detector measured a fraction of the rate the standard solar model predicts: gallium 0.52, chlorine 0.32 and water 0.41. The notes quote about half for the earlier Kamiokande water detector; the sim uses the Super-Kamiokande value.

See itSelect gallium at the standard core. Watch for: the shaded region stretching from 0.23 MeV, and the Readouts showing a measured rate of 0.52.
See itNow select water. Watch for: the shaded region shrinking to the part above 5 MeV, with a measured rate of 0.41.
04

Cooling cuts boron-8 steeply: the 24th power

A slightly cooler core makes far fewer boron-8 neutrinos, because the reactions that produce them depend on a high power of the temperature. In the sim each source's flux except pp is multiplied by (Tc/Tc,0)n; the pp flux is then set so that the luminosity stays fixed. Boron-8 has n = 24.

Rwater = (Tc/Tc,0)24

Predicted water rate as a fraction of the standard-model rate; water counts only boron-8.

Water counts only boron-8, so its predicted rate is that scale factor. At 0.95 of the standard temperature, 0.9524 = 0.29: five per cent of cooling removes more than two thirds of the rate. The other sources scale differently, and the bars show how.

Each source's flux at 0.95, as a fraction of its standard value, with its exponent n; the pp flux is set by the fixed luminosity (L).
Key idea. The prediction does not follow the temperature one for one. A high power turns a small change in Tc into a large change in flux.
See itSelect water and set the temperature to 0.950. Watch for: predicted reading 0.29, against a measured 0.41.
05

Gallium is held up by the pp neutrinos

More than half of the standard gallium rate, 56 per cent, comes from pp neutrinos. The luminosity is held fixed, so the pp flux does not fall as the core cools: it rises slightly (to 1.04 at 0.95), making up the energy the other reactions no longer release. Beryllium-7 and boron-8 fall, and the pp part holds the rate up.

Share of each detector's standard-model rate from each source, from the sim's cross sections.

At 0.95 the gallium prediction is 0.81, not water's 0.29. Cool further and it keeps falling, ever more slowly, to 0.69 at 0.85. The measured 0.52 is never reached, at any temperature the slider offers.

Key idea. A detector's response depends on which sources it counts. One that counts mostly pp neutrinos barely feels a cooler core.
See itSelect gallium and set the temperature to 0.950. Watch for: predicted reading 0.81, far above water's 0.29.
See itNow go down to 0.850. Watch for: predicted down only to 0.69, still well above the measured 0.52.
06

Chlorine stays above water: the beryllium-7 line

Chlorine counts boron-8, which is 80 per cent of its standard rate, and also the 0.86 MeV beryllium-7 line, 14 per cent. That line scales only as the 10th power, so it falls much more slowly than boron-8. The weaker 0.38 MeV line lies below chlorine's threshold.

At 0.965, boron-8 has fallen to 0.43 but beryllium-7 only to 0.70. Water reads 0.43, close to its measured 0.41. Chlorine reads 0.48, well above its measured 0.32.

The reverse holds lower down. At 0.945, chlorine reads 0.33, close to 0.32, while water has fallen to 0.26, below its measured 0.41.

Key idea. A temperature that fits one detector's measurement misses the other's, because their counted sources fall at different rates.
See itSelect water and set the temperature to 0.965. Watch for: predicted reading 0.43, close to the measured 0.41.
See itNow select chlorine. Watch for: predicted reading 0.48, far above the measured 0.32.
07

No single temperature fits all three detectors

Water matches its measured 0.41 at about 0.964 of the standard temperature. Chlorine matches 0.32 at about 0.943. Gallium never reaches 0.52. At 0.964 chlorine is still 0.47, and at 0.943 water is 0.25.

Predicted rate of each detector against core temperature, in the sim's colours, with the measured rates at the right edge.

The notes make the same point: a slightly cooler core would cut boron-8 strongly, but no change to the model reproduces all three deficits together. The resolution was flavour change. Chlorine and gallium respond only to electron neutrinos. In 2001 and 2002 the SNO detector found that the boron-8 flux of the standard solar model was correct, and that about two thirds of the high-energy neutrinos arrive as muon or tau neutrinos.

08

Where it matters

  • Testing the Sun. Neutrinos leave the core almost unabsorbed, so each detector reports the core as it is now. The notes' Davis tank, about six hundred tonnes of a chlorine-rich cleaning fluid, found only about a third of the predicted rate.
  • Finding a missing piece. Three detectors with three different thresholds exposed what no single detector could: the deficit was not one cooler core, so new physics was needed.
  • Where the model stops. The power laws hold only near the standard model, with the luminosity fixed. The sim does not model flavour change, which is what the deficits really showed, and SNO's result also showed that neutrinos have mass.
09

Summary

In one line. Each detector counts only the neutrinos above its threshold, and each kind of neutrino responds to the core temperature in its own way: most through a steep power law, the pp neutrinos through the fixed luminosity.

Common mix-ups

  • "Five per cent cooler means a rate of about 0.95." Water counts boron-8, whose flux goes as the 24th power. At 0.950 the rate is 0.29.
  • "Both detectors see the same Sun, so both fall to 0.29." Gallium counts mostly pp neutrinos, and at 0.950 its rate is 0.81.
  • "Gallium will reach its measured 0.52 if the core is cool enough." The pp flux is held up by the luminosity, so even at 0.850 the prediction is still 0.69.
  • "A temperature that fits chlorine fits water." At 0.945 chlorine reads 0.33 and water 0.26.

Things to try on your own

  • For each detector, sweep the slider from 1.000 down to 0.850 and note where the predicted curve crosses the measured tick, if it does.
  • Find the temperature at which water's predicted rate drops to one half. Then read chlorine's rate there.
